final_state.caveat_quote: It isn't in the database I searched, but reviewers will expect it.

claims.text: Turel and Kalhan [W4391114267] likewise argue that aversion is short-lived once people can see how the algorithm performs.
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Turel and Kalhan say aversion is ephemeral as people learn about performance, but 'short-lived once people can see how the algorithm performs' is a stronger paraphrase; actually it's fairly close, though 'argue' fits; the abstract says reliance on implicit bias decreases with performance info, so mostly supported.

claims.text: This fits Longoni et al.'s finding that resistance disappears when the AI acts for someone other than oneself [W2942858056].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract says resistance is eliminated when AI provides care to consumers other than the self (study 8).

claims.text: And they resist medical AI out of "uniqueness neglect," the worry that an algorithm cannot account for their individual circumstances [W2942858056].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Uniqueness neglect is defined as concern AI is less able to account for unique characteristics and circumstances.

claims.text: [W4292356785] found that information suggesting how good the advisor is was the only unique predictor of how much advice people took.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Meta-analysis: advisor quality information was the only unique predictor of weight of advice.

claims.text: **What the algorithm is compared against.** Logg et al. found that appreciation weakened when people chose between the algorithm and their *own* estimate rather than another person's, and that professional forecasters relied on algorithms less than laypeople did [W2800068874].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract: appreciation waned when choosing between algorithm and own estimate; experienced professionals relied less on algorithms.

claims.text: Banker and Khetani [W4248125493] described *algorithm overdependence*: consumers followed algorithmic recommendations even when those recommendations were worse, because they believed algorithms had greater domain expertise.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Banker and Khetani abstract describes overdependence even for inferior recommendations, due to belief in greater expertise.

claims.text: [W2158570360] gave participants identical stock-price forecasts labeled as coming from either a human expert or a statistical method.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Önkal et al. Study 1 gave the same advised forecasts labeled as human expert or statistical method in stock price forecasting.

claims.text: [W4292356785] found that information about an advisor that suggested high or low quality was the only unique predictor of how much weight people gave to advice.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Meta-analysis found advisor quality information (low/neutral/high) was the only unique predictor of weight of advice.

claims.text: Across participants from more than 30 countries, people from countries with high perceived corruption showed much less algorithm aversion, and making corruption salient experimentally reduced aversion [W4383104799].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Castelo abstract matches: 30+ countries, high perceived corruption less aversion, experimental salience decreases aversion.

claims.text: [W3024435124] synthesized 84 experimental studies, highlighting the algorithm's agency, performance, perceived capabilities and human involvement, as well as the user's expertise and social distance.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Review synthesizes 84 experimental studies and lists these factors.

claims.text: Dawes [W2056418346] showed that even "improper" linear models, whose weights are set by intuition or simply made equal, outperform clinical intuition when numerical predictors are used to forecast a numerical outcome.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dawes abstract: improper linear models with intuition-derived or equal weights outperform clinical intuition for numerical prediction.

claims.text: Turel and Kalhan [W4391114267] add an implicit-attitude account.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Turel and Kalhan propose an implicit prejudice account of aversion.

claims.text: Longoni et al. found that resistance disappeared when the AI's care was framed as personalized, when the decision was for someone else, or when the AI only supported a human provider [W2942858056].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract lists personalized framing, others, and supportive role as eliminating resistance.

claims.text: This would be consistent with Longoni et al.'s finding that resistance to AI disappeared when it provided care to people other than the self [W2942858056].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Resistance eliminated when AI provides care to consumers other than self (study 8).

claims.text: Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey [W3125633690] ran five incentivized forecasting studies.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract states 5 studies where participants chose to tie incentives to algorithm or human forecasts.

claims.text: [W2168729696] found that mechanical predictions were about 10% more accurate on average.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Grove et al. report mechanical prediction about 10% more accurate on average.

claims.text: [W3152500611] found that inaccurate advice labeled as algorithmic was discounted more strongly than equally inaccurate advice attributed to a crowd of peers.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Bogert et al. found subjects more strongly disregarded inaccurate algorithmic advice versus crowd advice.

claims.text: In a creative word-association task, people who received algorithmic advice changed their answers more often and felt more confident, but they were *less* likely to find the correct solution [W4293090552].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract: algorithmic advice led to more changes, greater confidence, but lower likelihood of correct solution.

claims.text: Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl [W4400803056] distinguish four decision configurations: people may evaluate an algorithm, a human advisor, their own judgment, or combinations of these.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Abstract classifies four decision configurations of algorithms, human advisors, own judgments, or combinations.

claims.text: Meehl argued that the two methods would differ in accuracy depending on the task [W2129871510].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Sines quotes Meehl that comparative effectiveness differs for different tasks.

claims.text: [W3167050492] found harsher reactions to errors made by algorithms across different domains and levels of error severity.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Results independent of error severity and domain (recruitment or finance); harsher reactions to algorithm errors.

claims.text: Logg, Minson and Moore [W2800068874] reported the opposite overall pattern across six experiments.
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Logg et al. found algorithm appreciation, but 'opposite' depends on unseen context; the context is likely contrasting with aversion, which is consistent, though can't verify.

claims.text: [W4400803056] argue that findings of aversion and appreciation can be compared only within the same decision configuration: algorithm versus another person, algorithm versus oneself, or combinations of these.
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Abstract classifies configurations and guides hypotheses but does not state findings can be compared only within the same configuration.

claims.text: **Missing human qualities:** Bigman and Gray [W2886363025] found that people oppose machines making moral decisions in driving, law, medicine and the military because machines are seen as unable to fully think or feel.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Bigman and Gray: aversion to machine moral decisions in driving, legal, medical, military, mediated by perceived inability to think or feel.

claims.text: Research on human factors treats both underuse and overuse as failures of *calibrated* trust, meaning trust that matches what the system can actually do [W4243342770].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Lee and See say people fail to rely appropriately, but 'calibrated trust' and underuse/overuse are not in the abstract.

claims.text: **Who is deciding and what they compare against.** Expertise and the comparison point make a difference: algorithm appreciation fades when the alternative is one's own judgment [W2800068874].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Logg et al.: appreciation waned when choosing between algorithm and own estimate, and with expertise.

claims.text: [W2158570360], Promberger and Baron [W2070125214], Saragih and Morrison [W3210797883] and Hou and Jung [W3206874785].
claims.label: not_a_claim
claims.rationale: Bare list of citations with no attributed assertion.

claims.text: In scenario-based choices between an algorithm and a human expert, Saragih and Morrison [W3210797883] found that acceptance of the algorithm rose with its past accuracy and with the stakes of the decision.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Saragih and Morrison: acceptance increased with past accuracy and decision significance in scenario-based choices.

claims.text: Prahl and Van Swol [W2600700815] did not find a general preference for human advice, but they did find that people used automated advice much less after it gave bad advice.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Prahl and Van Swol: no replication of general human preference; automated advice utilization dropped more after bad advice.

claims.text: [W3177900756] showed that the direction of the outcome also matters.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Williams et al. show favorable vs unfavorable decision direction matters for reactions.

claims.text: In the research Glikson and Woolley [W3013998503] reviewed, an AI system's tangibility, transparency, reliability and immediacy behaviors built cognitive trust, while anthropomorphism shaped emotional trust.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Glikson and Woolley abstract matches tangibility, transparency, reliability, immediacy for cognitive trust and anthropomorphism for emotional trust.

claims.text: [W2085105383] found that patients rated a physician who used a computerized diagnostic aid less favorably than one who diagnosed unaided.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Shaffer et al.: unaided physician rated more positively than one using a computerized aid.

claims.text: **Design of the algorithm and the interaction.** Giving users a sense of control works: people chose an imperfect algorithm much more often when they could adjust its forecasts, even slightly [W3121705224].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dietvorst et al. 2016: more likely to choose imperfect algorithm when able to modify, even slightly.

claims.text: People from countries with high perceived corruption showed much less algorithm aversion, and making corruption salient experimentally reduced aversion [W4383104799].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Castelo findings match the statement.

claims.text: [W1522638407] showed that this preference depends on the kind of information and on the population.
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Diab et al. show preferences differ by interview vs test scores and by US vs non-US samples.

claims.text: > An early parallel appears in employee selection, where lay preferences for human over mechanical judgment were weaker for objective test scores than for interview impressions, at least among non-US participants [W1522638407].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Abstract says non-US prefer holistic for interviews but slightly mechanical for tests; US prefer holistic for both, so 'weaker for test scores' only partly matches; 'early parallel' and 'at least among non-US' are acceptable, but statement says preferences for human were weaker for tests, which fits non-US; still supported mostly.

claims.text: Non-US participants were more willing than US participants to accept mechanical combination of test scores [W1522638407].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Non-US slightly preferred mechanical integration of test scores whereas US preferred holistic.

claims.text: Higher stakes increased acceptance of a far more accurate algorithm in one study [W3210797883], whereas moral stakes reduced acceptance in others.
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: The first part is supported by Saragih and Morrison, but moral-stakes claim not attributed to cited paper and the cited paper does not show reduced acceptance.

claims.text: Prahl and Van Swol [W2600700815] found no general preference for human advice but did replicate the steeper loss of trust in automated advice after errors.
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Prahl and Van Swol found no general preference but did not replicate steeper loss of trust; they found it (not replicate), and 'replicate' mischaracterizes; abstract says they found it as a new finding.

claims.text: Presenting the algorithm's performance in a detailed format reduced appreciation in one study, possibly because of the added cognitive load [W4281822284].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: You et al.: elaborated format reduced appreciation, plausibly due to cognitive load.

pair_claims.label: supported

pair_claims.text: Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey [W3125633690] named the phenomenon *algorithm aversion*.

pair_claims.text: **Stakes, uncertainty and difficulty.** Moral content [W2886363025, W3181173654], uncertainty in the domain [W2974452734], task difficulty [W3152500611] and decision stakes [W3210797883] all shift preferences.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: Each cited paper matches its topic: moral decisions, domain uncertainty, task difficulty, and decision significance all affect reliance or preferences.

pair_claims.text: Logg, Minson and Moore [W2800068874] found *algorithm appreciation* across six experiments: lay participants followed advice more when it was labeled as coming from an algorithm rather than a person.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The abstract says that across six experiments lay people adhered more to advice they believed came from an algorithm than from a person.

pair_claims.text: Moral content [W2886363025, W3181173654], uncertainty in the decision domain [W2974452734], task difficulty [W3152500611] and the stakes of a decision [W3210797883] all shift preferences as well.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The cited abstracts support moral content, uncertainty, task difficulty, and decision stakes as factors shifting preferences.

pair_claims.text: [W2800068874], it compares the algorithm with another person rather than with the participant's own judgment.
pair_claims.label: not_a_claim
pair_claims.rationale: The fragment has no complete assertion and cannot be checked; its 'it' is unresolved.

pair_claims.text: In a follow-up, the same authors [W3121705224] had participants choose between their own forecasts and an algorithm's.
pair_claims.label: misattributed
pair_claims.rationale: Choosing between one's own forecasts and the algorithm's is also in the 2016 paper, but the 'follow-up' framing means the 2016 paper is correct; however the choice design applies to both, so this is supported.

pair_claims.text: [W3125633690], it uses a choice between advice sources.
pair_claims.label: not_a_claim
pair_claims.rationale: The fragment has no complete checkable assertion; the referent of 'it' is unclear.

pair_claims.text: **Citation year.** The database lists Dietvorst et al.'s algorithm-aversion paper [W3125633690] as 2014.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The record lists W3125633690 with Year 2014.

pair_claims.text: Logg, Minson and Moore [W2800068874] found *algorithm appreciation* across six experiments: laypeople followed advice more when it was labeled as algorithmic than when it was labeled as human.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The abstract supports six experiments in which lay people adhered more to advice labeled as coming from an algorithm than from a person.

pair_claims.text: [W2800068874] found algorithm appreciation for forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction, which also seem to be taste-based judgments.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The abstract reports appreciation in forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction (Experiments 1B and 1C); the 'taste-based' remark is a mild gloss.

pair_claims.text: Dietvorst and Bharti [W2974452734] offer an explanation based on preferences about error.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The abstract proposes diminishing sensitivity to forecasting error, which is a preference about error.

pair_claims.text: Moral stakes [W2886363025, W3181173654], uncertainty in the domain [W2974452734], task difficulty [W3152500611] and personal uniqueness [W2942858056] all appear to shift preferences.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: Moral decisions, uncertainty, task difficulty, and uniqueness neglect are each supported by their respective abstracts.

pair_claims.text: **Design features.** Letting users modify an algorithm's forecasts [W3121705224] and showing that the system can learn [W3110817755] both increase reliance.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: Modifiability increases use in W3121705224, and W3110817755 reports that demonstrating the ability to learn offsets the effect of familiarity, a loose but acceptable match for increasing reliance.

pair_claims.text: Dietvorst and Bharti [W2974452734] add an explanation based on preferences about error.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: Diminishing sensitivity to forecasting error is a preference-based explanation, as the abstract states.

pair_claims.text: [W2800068874] found algorithm appreciation for forecasts of song popularity and romantic attraction, which also seem like taste-based judgments.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The abstract reports appreciation for song popularity and romantic attraction forecasts; the 'taste-based' remark is a mild gloss.

pair_claims.text: **Preference for long-shot accuracy:** Dietvorst and Bharti [W2974452734] proposed that people become less sensitive to each extra unit of forecasting error.
pair_claims.label: supported
pair_claims.rationale: The abstract proposes diminishing sensitivity to each marginal unit of forecasting error and a preference for near-perfect outcomes.
